source.title: Scaling Laws for Autoregressive Generative Modeling
source.authors: T. Henighan; J. Kaplan; Mor Katz; Mark Chen; Christopher Hesse; Jacob Jackson; Heewoo Jun; Tom B. Brown; Prafulla Dhariwal; Scott Gray; Chris Hallacy; Benjamin Mann; A. Radford; A. Ramesh; Nick Ryder; Daniel M. Ziegler; John D. Schulman; D. Amodei; Sam McCandlish

record.tranche_reason: The paper extends autoregressive cross-entropy scaling-law measurements to image, video, multimodal, and mathematical data, and also tests downstream image classification and architecture aspect ratios.
record.gate_note: The paper also cites language scaling results from other studies; those cited results are not recorded as this study's own rows. Values used only to select hyperparameters are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own autoregressive Transformer sweeps on images, video, image-text and math, and fits L(N), L(C), L(D) and Nopt(C). This tests V5 directly, and tests V3, V4, V6 and V7 in non-text settings. Its language results are cited from GPT-3 and Kaplan et al., so V1 (language) is not tested by its own data.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is largely right. Also add four points: classification keeps improving even as generative loss nears its irreducible value; the authors infer sub-linear data scaling (D∝N^0.4); math extrapolation depends on training loss, not size per se; and the L(C)/L(D) inconsistency's resolution (optimization becoming one-epoch efficient) is a hypothesis.
record.recipe_differences: Uses autoregressive Transformer cross-entropy scaling sweeps, closely matching the broad measurement approach, but applies it primarily to images, video, multimodal data, and math rather than testing language pretraining scaling directly. It also includes aspect-ratio scans, downstream fine-tuning, and dataset-size comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling exponents vary by modality, image resolution, and math difficulty. The paper reports small-model departures at higher image resolutions and an apparent inconsistency among L(D), L(C), and Nopt(C). Aspect-ratio optima differ across domains.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss vs context position follows a power-law+constant for video (and language per Kaplan) but not for images, where loss peaks at the first pixels and the image centre.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Power-law scaling of loss with context position is data-structure dependent, unlike N/C scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Image-text mutual information and infogain grow roughly logarithmically with model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multimodal mutual information scales as λ log(N/Nc).

record.problems: The authors state that the largest models in some sweeps had not converged, and that some small image/video models underperform the trends. They exclude two math extrapolation generators from main trends because of poor loss and overfitting. The compute-versus-dataset-size inconsistency remains unresolved. Reported uncertainty intervals are not provided.
record.rows_left_out: Language scaling results in Figures 1, 3, 5, and 15 are attributed to prior studies rather than new results. Omitted detailed per-image loss percentiles and individual examples (Figures 10, 17, and 20), per-frame video details beyond the final-frame trend (Figures 6 and 9), per-module math breakdowns (Figures 23, 26, and 27), and multimodal mutual-information results (Figures 12, 28, and 29), because these do not directly measure the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: All of it. Language loss scaling is only cited (GPT-3, Kaplan); there are no new language sweeps.
There is no held-out test of small-run fits predicting much larger runs. Only forecasts are given (e.g. video, 8x8 images).

Language setting not tested. Loss-minimising token count is not measured directly (it is inferred under a one-epoch assumption). Kaplan vs Hoffmann allocations are not compared. No critical-batch-size adjustment is made.
Language setting not tested. Only aspect ratio is varied; other architecture details are not. The size of the loss change across the range is not quantified in the text.
There is no broad multi-task downstream suite. The GPT-3 arithmetic/QA appendix is qualitative and cited-model based.
Parameter counting, LR schedule and fitting-method choices are not varied. A weight-decay effect on the math compute law is only suspected.

missing.what: Per-domain L(N) model-size fits (exponents, irreducible losses) for every domain, including the image model-size reducible-loss power laws.
Irreducible loss from L(D) vs L(C) agrees: 2013 vs 2023 nats/image (16x16) and 599 vs 602 (8x8).
Math in-distribution/interpolate model-size trends are distorted. Math training loss fits a power law less well, possibly due to the implicit curriculum.
The math compute law may be affected by weight decay. Compute is not adjusted for critical batch size.
Loss of individual images and of loss percentiles follows the same power-law+constant form as the mean.

record.verdict_notes: Henighan et al. is not an original source. Language curves (Figures 1, 3, 5, 15; Table 1 language row) are cited from Kaplan/GPT-3 and are not this study's evidence, so V1 gets no verdict. V3 and V4 are tested only outside text. The reader's V6 limits_scope on R14 and V5 limits_scope on R13 are removed: R14 supports predictability from loss, and R13 is a control. R18 is moved from V6 to V5 (transfer).

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not itself test natural-language pretraining scaling; it uses cited language results for comparison. Its own measurements cover model size and compute in several other domains and dataset size in selected experiments.
The paper fits scaling curves and discusses forecasting, but does not report a held-out test where a fit to small runs predicts substantially larger runs.

It measures optimal model size as a function of compute, but does not directly measure the empirically loss-minimizing token count at fixed compute or compare the Kaplan and Hoffmann allocations. Dataset-size implications are inferred under a one-epoch assumption.
The reported architecture scan varies aspect ratio (width/depth); it does not separately isolate all other architecture details.

It tests image, video, multimodal, and math settings, plus ImageNet fine-tuning and selected dataset-size effects. It does not test repeated-data training as a distinct regime or broad transfer across many downstream tasks.

Downstream evidence is primarily ImageNet classification after image-model pretraining, plus math performance by difficulty and training loss; it does not establish predictability across a broad set of downstream tasks.

It examines differing scaling exponents across domains and resolutions and an apparent inconsistency among dataset-size, compute, and optimal-model-size trends. It does not systematically vary every fitting choice named in the version.

conditions.value: 16 sequential frames; 16x16 VQ codes per frame

rows.measure: Reducible loss per frame versus model size and compute
rows.value: The paper reports a power-law trend with model size and compute; it estimates that a model around 10^13 parameters and compute around 10^4 PF-days would reach a few nats/frame.
rows.note: Aggregate trends; the first frame is omitted from the model-size plot because it is treated as an image-modeling problem.

rows.subject: Mathematical problem-solving Transformers (aggregate sweep)
rows.size_stated: various; model sizes are reported in the paper
rows.operation_detail: Measured cross-entropy loss on procedurally generated math problems across model sizes and compute budgets.
rows.measure: Test cross-entropy loss versus model size and compute
rows.value: The paper reports power-law-plus-constant fits; the fits vary with difficulty level.
rows.note: Aggregate sweep. Two probability extrapolation generators with poor loss were excluded from the main trends because they would dominate them.
rows.check: Math, not language; drop V1. Add V7 because the exponents and offsets vary with difficulty level (Figure 3). Excludes two probability generators.

rows.subject: Multimodal image-text Transformers (aggregate sweeps)
rows.size_stated: various; model sizes are reported in the paper
rows.operation_detail: Measured multimodal cross-entropy losses across model sizes and compute budgets.
rows.value: The paper reports power-law-plus-constant fits for model-size and compute scaling.
rows.note: The paper reports text and image metrics separately; this row records the stated aggregate finding rather than assigning flattened table coefficients to individual metrics.
rows.check: Multimodal, not language; drop V1. The text-loss L(N) fits are pure power laws with very small exponents (0.037/0.039).

rows.subject: Autoregressive Transformer model families (aggregate across domains)
rows.size_stated: various; model sizes are reported in the paper
rows.operation_detail: Selected models on the compute-efficient loss frontier and fitted optimal model size as a function of compute.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal parameter count Nopt versus training compute C
rows.value: Nopt(C) ∝ C^β, with β approximately 0.7; individual domain fits shown in Figure 16 have exponents from 0.643 to 0.752.
rows.note: The authors describe the trend as remarkably similar across modalities. They infer dataset-size implications from this relation rather than measuring an optimal token allocation directly.
rows.check: Non-text domains only. Token allocation is inferred (D∝N^0.4 under one epoch), not measured. The per-domain exponent range in Figures 16/18 is 0.641-0.752, not 0.643-0.752. The 0.73 language value in Table 1 is cited from Kaplan et al.

rows.subject: Image, math, and text-to-image Transformer aspect-ratio scans
rows.size_stated: 27M parameters for the text-to-image scan; other scan sizes not stated in the text
rows.operation_detail: Compared converged loss across width/depth aspect ratios at fixed model size.
rows.measure: Converged loss versus architecture aspect ratio
rows.value: The text states that image and math models perform optimally at aspect ratio approximately 5, and that their optimal ratio is at least 10 times smaller than that for language.
rows.note: The study identifies a domain-dependent optimum but does not quantify the size of loss changes across the full aspect-ratio range.
rows.check: Non-text domains only. The 27M text-to-image scan is one of several scans. Math aspect-ratio scans used a different mmlp/mattn than the main math models.

rows.subject: Randomly initialized 32x32 image Transformers
rows.size_stated: various; model sizes are reported in the paper
rows.operation_detail: Trained on the ImageNet classification task without generative pretraining.
rows.measure: Classification loss and top-1 error rate versus parameter count
rows.value: The paper reports that the from-scratch models do not follow the pretrained models' smooth trend into the larger-model regime and exhibit overfitting; small models receive almost no benefit from pretraining.
rows.note: Comparator to the pretrained fine-tuning results.
rows.check: From-scratch classifiers are a control for the pretraining comparison and do not measure a scaling-law version. They should not carry a V5 limits_scope label.

rows.subject: Mathematical problem-solving Transformers (aggregate across sizes)
rows.size_stated: various; model sizes are reported in the paper
rows.operation_detail: Compared interpolation and extrapolation loss and accuracy at matched training loss across model sizes.
rows.measure: Test loss and accuracy at different difficulty levels
rows.baseline: Models of different sizes at the same training loss
rows.value: Models of different sizes perform about equally on the test distributions when training loss is held fixed; larger models improve mainly insofar as they improve training-distribution performance.
rows.note: Aggregate comparison across model sizes and difficulty levels.
rows.check: Test performance at each difficulty is predicted by training loss, independent of model size. This matches V6's 'or with pretraining loss', so the state should be observed, not partial.

rows.subject: Mathematical problem-solving Transformers (aggregate dataset-size sweep)
rows.operation_detail: Varied training dataset size and recorded minimum test losses.
rows.value: The paper reports power-law fits; the displayed exponents are 0.512 for interpolation loss and 0.239 for extrapolation loss.
rows.note: The plotted fits are reported for the two test distributions separately.
rows.check: Math, not language; drop V1. Interpolate vs extrapolate is a test-distribution difference, not a fitting choice, so drop V7. Model uses mmlp=4.

rows.subject: Pixel-level image Transformers (aggregate dataset-size and compute comparison)
rows.size_stated: various; model sizes are reported in the paper
rows.operation_detail: Compared dataset-size loss L(D), compute loss L(C), and the compute-parametrized dataset-size trend L(D(C)).

conditions.value: learning curves compared with early-stopped dataset-size trends

rows.measure: Loss versus dataset size and compute
rows.baseline: Learning curves must lie above L(D)
rows.value: The extrapolated L(C) trend intersects and passes below L(D(C)); the paper concludes that at least one of L(D), L(C), or Nopt(C) must break down by that point.
rows.uncertainty: The paper illustrates sensitivity to changing the Nopt(C) exponent by ±5%.
rows.note: The authors present this as an apparent inconsistency and offer increasing optimization efficiency as a possible explanation, not a demonstrated resolution.
rows.check: Drop V1. The breakdown is a projected intersection, not an observed bend. Projections are very sensitive to ±5% in the Nopt exponent.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6; Figure 14. Figure 15 supplies the cited language comparison.

rows.subject: Pixel-level image Transformers (aggregate small-model results)
rows.operation_detail: Compared small-model losses with the fitted model-size and compute scaling trends.
rows.measure: Test loss versus model size and compute
rows.value: The smallest models underperform the trends at resolutions greater than 8x8; the paper speculates that they have difficulty using positional encodings or attending to long contexts.
rows.note: This is a stated departure from the fitted trend for a particular model-size and resolution range.
rows.check: Drop V1. This is an observed small-model departure from the single power-law fit at high resolutions and for video.

rows.subject: YFCC100M-pretrained image Transformers evaluated on ImageNet
rows.size_stated: various; model sizes are reported in the paper
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated image models trained on YFCC100M against the ImageNet data distribution.
rows.measure: ImageNet generative test loss versus model size and YFCC100M training loss
rows.value: The paper reports that ImageNet loss depends on YFCC100M loss and not otherwise on model size, and that ImageNet loss appears to follow a power-law-plus-constant trend with model size.
rows.note: This is an evaluation on a distribution different from the training distribution; the authors note that it does not by itself identify the ImageNet entropy.
rows.check: This is generative loss on a shifted distribution (ImageNet), i.e. transfer, not a downstream task, so it bears on V5 rather than V6.
